practice.intro: One kid better. One class better. The building better. Pick the choice that fits the four words best.

items.question: You're in a group project. One member hasn't done their part, and it's due Friday. What's the best first step?

choices.text: Do their part yourself and say nothing.
Wait until the day it's due, then tell the teacher.
Leave their part blank so everyone sees it.
Ask them today what they can finish, and set a time to check back.

hints: Which one gives them a real chance to fix it?
Which one still has time left in it?
items.reasoning: Start with the person, and start early. If nothing changes, then bring in the teacher. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.A: Covering for them in silence wears you out and fixes nothing for next time.
distractors.B: By then, nobody has time to fix anything.
distractors.C: A blank part hurts the whole group's grade, yours too.

items.question: You left your finished homework at home. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell your teacher at the start of class and ask when you can bring it in.
Say nothing and hope it isn't collected.
Say you never got the assignment.
Redo it in a rush during class while notes are going.

hints: Which one is honest and quick?
Which one gives your teacher a chance to help?
items.reasoning: Owning it early usually costs less than hiding it. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.B: Hoping isn't a plan, and it usually gets noticed.
distractors.C: That trades a small problem for a trust problem.
distractors.D: Now you're missing today's work too.

items.question: Practice runs late tonight, and an assignment is due tomorrow. When do you deal with it?

choices.text: After practice, whenever you get home.
In the morning, on the bus.
Now: look at it and plan when you'll do each part.
You don't. Practice is a good enough reason.

hints: When do you have the most choices?
Which one leaves room for something to go wrong?
items.reasoning: A busy night needs a plan made before it starts. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.A: Late and tired is the hardest time to start something.
distractors.B: The bus isn't a desk, and there's no time left if it takes longer.
distractors.D: Being busy is real. The work still counts, so plan around it.

items.question: You borrowed a classmate's calculator for the quiz. The bell rings. What do you do?

choices.text: Keep it until tomorrow. They probably won't need it.
Give it back before you leave the room.
Leave it on your desk for them to find.
Hand it to a friend to return.

hints: Whose calculator is it?
Which one makes sure it ends up back in their hands?
items.reasoning: Return what you borrow, the way you got it, when you said you would. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.A: They might need it next period, and that's their call, not yours.
distractors.C: Desks get cleared and things get picked up. It might not be there.
distractors.D: Now two people are responsible for it, so nobody is.

items.question: You got a quiz question wrong, and you're not sure why. What helps most?

choices.text: Forget it. The quiz is over.
Decide the question was unfair.
Memorize the right letter.
Find the right answer and figure out where your thinking went off.

hints: Which one helps on the next question like it?
Is the letter the point, or the reason?
items.reasoning: A wrong answer you understand is worth more than a right one you guessed. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.A: The same skill comes back on the next quiz.
distractors.B: Maybe, but you still won't know it next time.
distractors.C: The letter changes next time. The reason doesn't.

items.question: You said you'd help at a club event Saturday, and now you can't make it. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell the person in charge as soon as you know.
Just don't show up. They'll figure it out.
Tell them Saturday morning.
Send a friend in your place without asking.

hints: When does the group have the most time to adjust?
Which one treats your word like it matters?
items.reasoning: Plans change. Saying so early keeps your word worth something. That's Be Responsible.

distractors.B: Somebody planned around you, and now they find out too late.
distractors.C: Same news, less time to fix it.
distractors.D: They planned for you, and they may need something your friend can't do.

items.question: Your teacher is giving directions, and your friend keeps talking to you. What do you do?

choices.text: Talk back quietly. It's only a minute.
Say "after" and keep listening.
Ignore the directions and ask the teacher later.
Tell your friend, loudly, to be quiet.

hints: Which one gets you the directions and keeps your friend?
Which one doesn't pull anyone else in?
items.reasoning: Listening while someone talks to the room respects them and the people around you. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: Then you both miss it, and the teacher has to say it again.
distractors.C: The teacher already said it once, to everyone.
distractors.D: Now the whole room is listening to you instead.

items.question: You're late for class, and the people in front of you in the hallway are walking slowly. What do you do?

choices.text: Push through them.
Yell at them to hurry up.
Say "excuse me" and go around when there's room.
Turn around and take the long way.

hints: Which one gets you there without bumping anyone?
What would you want from the person behind you?
items.reasoning: Two words and a little patience get you there without anyone getting hurt. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: Pushing in a crowded hall is how people get knocked down.
distractors.B: They might not know you're there. Yelling starts something.

items.question: Lunch is over. Your table has trash on it, and not all of it is yours. What do you do?

choices.text: Clean up your spot and a little extra.
Leave it. It isn't all yours.
Leave it for the custodians. That's their job.
Slide it down to the next table.

hints: Who sits there next?
Which one leaves the place better than you found it?
items.reasoning: Shared spaces work when everyone leaves them a little better. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.B: Somebody has to start, and the next group sits in it either way.
distractors.C: They take care of the whole building. A minute of yours saves a lot of theirs.
distractors.D: That just hands the mess to someone else.

items.question: A classmate who's still learning English stops in the middle of a sentence to find a word. What do you do?

choices.text: Finish the sentence for them.
Laugh to lighten the mood.
Start talking so they don't feel put on the spot.
Wait, and give them the time.

hints: Whose idea is it?
What does waiting tell them?
items.reasoning: Giving someone time says their idea is worth hearing. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: You might guess wrong, and it's their thought to finish.
distractors.B: A laugh can land as laughing at them.
distractors.C: Taking over says their turn is done.

items.question: An adult who isn't your teacher stops you in the hallway and asks where you're headed. What do you do?

choices.text: Keep walking. They're not your teacher.
Give a smart answer.
Tell them where you're going and show your pass.
Say it's none of their business.

hints: Who are the adults in the building there for?
Which one gets you on your way fastest?
items.reasoning: Every adult in the building looks out for every student in it. A straight answer takes ten seconds. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: They're responsible for you too, and now a quick question becomes a bigger deal.
distractors.B: A joke at an adult's expense turns ten seconds into ten minutes.
distractors.D: Asking is part of their job, and a straight answer ends it fastest.

items.question: You think a grade on your paper is wrong. What's the best way to handle it?

choices.text: Argue about it in front of the class.
Ask your teacher, privately, to go over it with you.
Complain about it in the group chat.
Let it go and stay mad.

hints: Where can a real conversation happen?
Which one could actually change something?
items.reasoning: A calm, private question gets a real answer, and sometimes a fix. That's Be Respectful.

distractors.A: An audience makes everyone defend a side instead of looking at the paper.
distractors.C: The group chat can't change your grade.
distractors.D: If it might be wrong, it's worth one calm question.

items.question: A new student is standing in the hallway, staring at their schedule and looking lost. What do you do?

choices.text: Keep walking. Someone else will help.
Point in a general direction.
Ask where they're headed, and show them if it's on your way.
Laugh about it with your friends.

hints: What would have helped you on your first day?
Which one takes thirty seconds?
items.reasoning: Being new is hard. A little help on the first day is remembered for a long time. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: Everyone thinks that, and that's how people stay lost.
distractors.B: Better than nothing, but a big building is easy to get lost in.

items.question: Someone drops their books in a crowded hallway, and people laugh. What do you do?

choices.text: Laugh too. It was kind of funny.
Step around them and keep going.
Take a video.
Stop and help pick them up.

hints: How would it feel to be the one on the floor?
Which one changes the moment?
items.reasoning: One person helping changes how the whole hallway sees it. That's Be Kind.

distractors.B: Stepping around says you saw it and didn't care.
distractors.C: A video makes a bad moment last a lot longer.

items.question: Your group lost points because of one person's mistake, and they feel terrible. What do you say?

choices.text: "Thanks a lot."
"It happens. Let's get the next one."
Nothing. Let them sit with it.
Tell the rest of the group whose fault it was.

hints: They already know. What do they need now?
Which one helps the group do better next time?
items.reasoning: Everybody messes up. How the group responds decides what happens next. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: They already feel bad. Piling on doesn't fix the score.
distractors.D: Everyone already knows, so it only makes things worse.

items.question: A friend made the team, and you got cut. What do you do?

choices.text: Congratulate them, even if it stings.
Avoid them for a while.
Say the coach plays favorites.
Tell them they only made it on luck.

hints: Can you be disappointed and happy for them at the same time?
Which one keeps the friendship?
items.reasoning: You can feel disappointed and still be glad for a friend. That's Be Kind.

distractors.B: They didn't do anything to you.
distractors.C: That takes something from them and doesn't change the roster.
distractors.D: It takes something from them and gives you nothing back.

items.question: A classmate has been out for a couple of weeks. It's their first day back. What could you do?

choices.text: Ask where they've been, in front of everyone.
Tell them it's good to see them, and offer your notes.
Say nothing and act like nothing happened.
Tell them how far behind they are.

hints: What would make walking back in easier?
Which one doesn't make them explain anything?
items.reasoning: Making it easy to come back is one of the kindest things you can do. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: Why they were out is theirs to share, or not.
distractors.C: Saying nothing can feel like nobody noticed they were gone.
distractors.D: They already know, and it makes coming back harder.

items.question: In your group, the quiet person said something smart, and nobody heard it. What do you do?

choices.text: Use the idea as your own.
Let it go. They should speak up.
Wait for the teacher to notice.
Say "Wait, say that again" so the group hears it.

hints: Whose idea was it?
Which one makes them more likely to talk next time?
items.reasoning: Making room for a quiet voice makes the whole group smarter. That's Be Kind.

distractors.A: That's taking credit for their thinking.
distractors.B: Some people need a door held open first.
distractors.C: You're right there. The teacher isn't.

items.question: The fire alarm goes off. Your friend wants to stop at their locker first. What do you do?

choices.text: Leave with your class, the way you practiced.
Go with your friend. It'll be quick.
Stay in the room until you know it's real.
Leave, but split off from your class to find your friends.

hints: Who needs to know where you are?
Is there ever time to check whether it's real?
items.reasoning: Every alarm is real until an adult says it isn't, and your teacher has to count you. That's Be Safe.

distractors.B: Lockers can wait. In a real fire, seconds matter.
distractors.C: You can't tell from inside, and waiting costs time.
distractors.D: If you're not with your class, people have to go looking for you.

items.question: Kids are shoving each other on the stairs as a joke. What do you do?

choices.text: Join in. It's just fooling around.
Stay out of it and keep to the side.
Shove back if one of them bumps you.
Stop on the stairs and watch.

hints: What happens if someone loses their footing on stairs?
Which one keeps you out of the way of a fall?
items.reasoning: Stairs turn a joke into an injury fast. That's Be Safe.

distractors.A: One slip on the stairs and it isn't a joke anymore.
distractors.C: Now there's more shoving, not less.
distractors.D: Stopping on the stairs makes a pile-up more likely.

items.question: Someone you only know online asks what school you go to. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell them. What's the harm?
Send a picture so they know what you look like.
Give them the name of a different school.
Don't share it, and tell an adult if they keep asking.

hints: What could someone do with where you are every day?
Which one keeps you in control?
items.reasoning: Where you are every day is information to keep to yourself. That's Be Safe.

distractors.A: Your school tells a stranger where to find you.
distractors.B: Now they have your face too.
distractors.C: A made-up answer keeps the conversation going. Ending it is safer.

items.question: A friend hits their head in gym. They say they're fine, but they seem dizzy. What do you do?

choices.text: Take their word for it. They know how they feel.
Tell them to walk it off.
Tell the teacher right away.
Wait and see if they get worse.

hints: Who should decide whether a head injury is okay?
What does dizzy tell you?
items.reasoning: With a head injury, an adult decides, not the person who got hit. That's Be Safe.

distractors.A: People who hit their head often can't tell how hurt they are.
distractors.B: Walking it off is for a stubbed toe, not a head.
distractors.D: Waiting can make it worse. Telling someone costs nothing.

items.question: You signed out to the bathroom. A friend texts you to meet at the vending machines instead. What do you do?

choices.text: Go where your pass says, and come straight back.
Meet them for a minute. Nobody will notice.
Go, then say the bathroom line was long.
Stay out until the period's almost over.

hints: If the fire alarm went off right now, where would adults look for you?
Which choice makes your pass true?
items.reasoning: Your pass tells adults where to find you if something happens. Being where you said you'd be keeps you safe. That's Be Safe.

distractors.B: If something happens, they'll look where your pass says, and you won't be there.
distractors.C: Now it's a story you have to keep straight, and people stop trusting you.
distractors.D: Class keeps going without you, and every extra minute is harder to explain.

items.question: Your friends dare you to try an online challenge that looks dangerous. What do you do?

choices.text: Do it. Everyone else is.
Do a safer version for the video.
Pass, and suggest something else to do.
Film someone else doing it instead.

hints: What does the challenge get you, and what could it cost?
Is there a way to say no and keep your friends?
items.reasoning: A good group of friends can handle a no. That's Be Safe.

distractors.A: If everyone's doing it, everyone's taking the same risk.
distractors.B: A "safer" version of a dangerous thing is still a gamble.
distractors.D: Filming it can push someone else into getting hurt.
